title: FAR U4·W1 — Revenue Recognition (ASC 606) (CPA Core)
lessonHtml:
Cold open — one model for all revenue

ASC 606 replaced dozens of industry rules with a single five-step model for recognizing revenue from contracts with customers. For MBG it is the engine behind construction revenue — the contract assets and liabilities from FAR Unit 1 and the percentage-of-completion the auditor scrutinizes both flow from this model. Master the five steps and the construction application falls out.

Step 1 — identify the contract

A contract exists when it has commercial substance, the parties have approved it and are committed, rights to goods/services and payment terms are identifiable, and collection is probable. If collection is not probable, there is no contract for revenue purposes and any cash received is a deposit (a liability) until the criteria are met. Contracts can be combined when negotiated as a package.

Step 2 — identify the performance obligations

A performance obligation is a promise to transfer a distinct good or service. A good or service is distinct if the customer can benefit from it on its own (or with readily available resources) and it is separately identifiable from other promises in the contract. A construction contract is usually a single performance obligation — the many activities (site work, framing, finishing) are integrated into one combined output, the building — so they are not accounted for separately.

Step 3 — determine the transaction price

The transaction price is the consideration the entity expects to be entitled to. It includes variable consideration (incentives, penalties, change orders, claims) estimated by the expected value or most likely amount, but constrained so revenue is recognized only to the extent a significant reversal is not probable. The price is also adjusted for a significant financing component (the time value of money when payment timing is far from transfer), noncash consideration (at fair value), and consideration payable to the customer (usually a reduction of revenue).

Step 4 — allocate the transaction price

When a contract has multiple performance obligations, the transaction price is allocated to each in proportion to its standalone selling price (SSP) — the price at which the entity would sell that good or service separately. When an SSP is not observable, it is estimated (adjusted market assessment, expected cost plus margin, or, as a residual, only in limited cases). A discount is generally allocated proportionately across all obligations unless evidence shows it relates to specific ones.

Step 5 — recognize revenue as obligations are satisfied

Revenue is recognized when (or as) the entity satisfies a performance obligation by transferring control. Control transfers either at a point in time (most goods — when the customer obtains physical possession, legal title, risks/rewards, and has accepted the asset) or over time. An obligation is satisfied over time if any one of three criteria is met: the customer simultaneously receives and consumes the benefits; the entity creates or enhances an asset the customer controls; or the entity creates an asset with no alternative use and has an enforceable right to payment for performance to date.

Over-time recognition and construction

A typical construction contract meets the over-time criteria (the contractor builds on the customer's land, or the asset has no alternative use plus a right to payment), so MBG recognizes revenue over time using a measure of progress — an input method (cost-to-cost is the most common) or an output method (units or milestones). Worked example: a $5,000,000 contract with $3,000,000 of costs incurred against $4,000,000 of total estimated costs is 75% complete by cost-to-cost, so MBG recognizes $3,750,000 of revenue to date. When total costs are not reliably estimable, revenue is recognized only to the extent of recoverable costs until the estimate becomes reliable; an expected loss on the whole contract is recognized immediately.

Contract costs

Two cost types are capitalized rather than expensed. Incremental costs of obtaining a contract (a sales commission that would not have been incurred otherwise) are capitalized if the entity expects to recover them (with a practical expedient to expense them if the amortization period is one year or less). Costs to fulfill a contract (that are not in another standard) are capitalized when they relate directly to the contract, generate or enhance resources used to satisfy it, and are expected to be recovered. Both are amortized as the related revenue is recognized.

Special issues

Several recurring patterns: in a principal-versus-agent question, a principal controls the good/service before transfer and reports gross revenue, while an agent arranges for another party and reports only its net commission. A warranty that is merely assurance the product works is a cost accrual (not a separate obligation), but a service-type warranty the customer can buy separately is a distinct performance obligation. Licenses of intellectual property are recognized over time (a right to access) or at a point in time (a right to use) depending on whether the IP changes over the license period. Bill-and-hold and consignment arrangements turn on who controls the goods.

Contract modifications

A modification (a change order, common in construction) is treated three ways. If it adds distinct goods/services at their standalone price, it is a separate contract. If it adds distinct goods/services but not at standalone price, it is accounted for prospectively (terminate the old, create a new contract for the remaining work). If the remaining goods/services are not distinct (part of a single performance obligation, like most construction change orders), the modification is folded into the existing contract with a cumulative catch-up adjustment to revenue. Distinguishing these is a frequent exam and practice point for a contractor.

Presentation and disclosure

ASC 606 also reshapes presentation. A contract asset arises when the entity has performed but its right to payment is conditional on something other than the passage of time (MBG's underbillings); a receivable is an unconditional right to payment; and a contract liability arises when the customer pays before the entity performs (overbillings or deposits). Required disclosures include disaggregated revenue, the opening and closing contract balances, the remaining performance obligations (backlog), and the significant judgments made — the transparency that lets a reader of MBG's statements see how much work is sold but not yet earned.

CMA bridge

FAR Unit 1 introduced the contract assets (underbillings) and contract liabilities (overbillings) that ASC 606 produces; this unit supplies the full five-step engine behind them. The cost-to-cost measure of progress is the same percentage-of-completion the CMA WIP accounting computes and the auditor re-performs — revenue recognition is where the construction numbers originate.

Practice and recap

  1. Apply the five steps: identify the contract, the performance obligations, the transaction price, allocate by standalone selling price, and recognize as control transfers.
  2. Estimate variable consideration (expected value or most likely amount) subject to the constraint; adjust for significant financing and consideration payable to the customer.
  3. Recognize over time when one of the three criteria is met; use cost-to-cost for construction; book an expected contract loss immediately.
  4. Capitalize incremental costs to obtain and costs to fulfill; classify modifications as separate, prospective, or cumulative catch-up.

Recap: ASC 606's five-step model recognizes revenue as control transfers — a construction contract is usually one performance obligation satisfied over time, so a $5,000,000 job that is 75% complete by cost-to-cost recognizes $3,750,000; variable consideration is constrained, the transaction price is allocated by standalone selling price, expected losses are booked immediately, and change orders are separate, prospective, or a cumulative catch-up depending on whether the added work is distinct.

flashcards.back: 1) Identify the contract; 2) identify performance obligations; 3) determine the transaction price; 4) allocate by standalone selling price; 5) recognize revenue as control transfers.
The customer can benefit from the good/service on its own AND it is separately identifiable from other promises in the contract.
Estimated by expected value or most likely amount, CONSTRAINED so revenue is recognized only to the extent a significant reversal is not probable.
Customer simultaneously receives/consumes benefits; entity creates/enhances an asset the customer controls; OR no alternative use + enforceable right to payment for performance to date.
Costs incurred ÷ total estimated costs = % complete; applied to the transaction price (e.g., 75% of $5,000,000 = $3,750,000).
Recognized immediately and in full when total estimated costs exceed the contract price.
A principal controls the good/service before transfer and reports gross revenue; an agent arranges for another and reports only its net commission.
Separate contract (distinct + standalone price); prospective (distinct, not standalone); cumulative catch-up (not distinct — typical construction change order).

questions.q: The five steps of ASC 606 begin by:
choices: Identifying the contract with a customer
questions.explain: Step 1 is identifying the contract; recognition is the final step.

questions.q: Variable consideration is included in the transaction price:
choices: Only to the extent a significant reversal is not probable (the constraint)
questions.explain: Variable consideration is estimated but constrained to avoid a probable significant reversal.

questions.q: A construction contract is typically recognized:
choices: Over time, using a measure of progress
At a point in time at completion
Only when the building is sold
questions.explain: Construction usually meets an over-time criterion (no alternative use + right to payment, or customer-controlled asset).

questions.q: A $5,000,000 contract has incurred $3,000,000 of $4,000,000 total estimated costs. Revenue recognized to date (cost-to-cost) is:
An expected loss on a contract is:
questions.explain: A provision for the entire expected loss is recognized as soon as it is probable.

questions.q: The transaction price is allocated to multiple performance obligations based on:
questions.explain: Allocation is in proportion to each obligation's standalone selling price.

questions.q: An entity that controls a good before transferring it to the customer is a(n):
questions.explain: A principal controls the good before transfer and reports gross revenue; an agent reports net.
